title: How Talk Does Things in Schools
author: Rod Naquin
summary: Drawing on psycholinguistics, philosophy, and organizational theory, Naquin argues that conversation in schools is not merely the setting for educational work, it is the work itself. He builds from Garrod and Anderson's 1987 finding that dialogue partners actively construct shared vocabulary through iterative exchange (rather than arriving with one) and Fernando Flores's "conversations for action" framework, in which language creates commitments and most breakdowns occur at specific failed joints in the request/commitment/completion cycle. The practical upshot: shared professional vocabulary like "rigor" or "student-centered" cannot be assumed after a meeting, and talk that generates no clear request or commitment produces no action, however busy it feels. Naquin calls the deliberate attention to how talk works "conversational craft."
points: Conversation is not the container for educational work but the work itself, curriculum, culture, and thinking are all downstream of talk.
Shared meaning is an achievement, not a precondition: partners build it iteratively, so meetings can feel productive while shared understanding is actually absent.

Ambiguous professional vocabulary ("rigor," "student-centered," "engagement") carries different mental models for different people, and the divergence stays invisible until it produces action failures.
Flores's framework identifies specific joint failures, unclear requests, uncommitted responses, insincere commitments, incomplete actions, undeclared completions, where talk fails to generate action.
"Conversational craft" is a learnable, reflective technical practice that most professional development ignores, yet it determines whether a school's abundant talk moves anything forward.
quotes: Walk into any school and almost everything you observe is downstream of talk. Teachers build curriculum in planning meetings. Principals shape culture through the phrases they repeat. Students learn to think by speaking before they write. We tend to treat conversation as the setting in which educational work happens. It might be more accurate to say it is the work.

The default assumption is that talk transmits ideas — that meaning travels from one mind to another like a document passed across a table. Meaning is not transferred. It is built, jointly, in the live act of speaking and responding.

The word "rigor" means something different to the department chair than to the new teacher across the table. "Student-centered" carries one mental model for one person and something else entirely for another. The conversation feels productive. The shared ground isn't actually there.

A department meeting where everyone shares ideas but no one makes a clear request is not just an inefficient meeting — it is a meeting where talk, for all its apparent activity, did nothing. No action was generated. No commitment was taken.
What this body of work ultimately argues is that talk in schools needs to be understood as a technical practice, not just a social one.
It is not enough to create space for talk. The question is whether the talk being done is the kind that builds shared ground, generates real commitment, and moves people toward action.
